say: Today you are machine builders and machine breakers. Every machine has a secret rule. In Secondary 1 the rule is written with a letter, like 3n + 2, and that is all algebra is: a machine written down.
Notice it, test it, explain why. Today we test our rules in code.
I am a machine. Call out a number and I will tell you what comes out. You say 3, I say 8. You say 7, I say 12. What is my rule?
Which numbers did you choose to call out? Which ones helped you most?
My machine does times 3, then add 2. If you type 4, what will it say? Write your prediction before we run the code.
If I swap the steps, add 2 first and then times 3, will 4 give the same answer? Thumbs up or down.
stuck: Stuck building: put the * block inside the + block, then put “answer” in the first gap of the *.
Stuck cracking a rule: ask for IN 0, 1, 2, 3. How much does OUT go up each time?
Finished early: swap jobs (the Go further what-if), make a three-step machine, or put ask and say in a forever loop.

say: “IN goes up by 1 and OUT goes up by 4 each time. That is what times 4 does. 4 × 1 is 4 but OUT is 7, so I add 3. Rule: 4n + 3. Check: 4 × 4 + 3 = 19.”
“Machine A adds 2 then times 5; machine B times 5 then adds 2. For 4: (4 + 2) × 5 = 30 and 4 × 5 + 2 = 22. Same steps, different order, different answer. The brackets show what happens first.”
“5n − 4 = 31. The machine did times 5, then take away 4. I undo the last step first: 31 + 4 = 35. Then undo times 5: 35 ÷ 5 = 7. Check: 7 × 5 − 4 = 31.”

do: Ask: “Did you check your rule on every pair, not just the first?”
Ask: “What was the last step? What is its opposite?”
Ask: “How could the computer check your answer?”
stuck: Hint 1: “How much does OUT go up when IN goes up by 1? That is the × part.”
Hint 2: “Draw the machine boxes. Write the OUT at the end and go backwards.”
Hint 3: “Put your answer back into the machine. Do you get the OUT?”

say: “To solve 4n + 7 = 43, Ravi tries n = 1, 2, 3 … like the computer. Mei runs the machine backwards. Which way is better, and when?”
ask: “To solve 4n + 7 = 43, Ravi tries n = 1, 2, 3 … like the computer. Mei runs the machine backwards. Which way is better, and when?”

Both give n = 9. Running backwards is quicker by hand and works for big numbers. Trying every n is easy to code and also works when there is no easy backwards step (like n × n + n = 90), but it is slow by hand and must stop if there is no whole-number answer. We undo the last step first because it was the last thing done, like taking off shoes before socks.

say: “Today you wrote rules with a letter, ran machines backwards and let the computer search. That is the start of Secondary 1 algebra, and you explained it in your own words. Well done, inquirers!”

p6l4-title.note: Objective: Find the rule of a function machine from a table and write it with a letter (OUT = 3n + 2); see that the order of steps matters and use brackets; solve simple equations by running the machine backwards (undo the last step first) and check forwards; build an input-rule-output program and use a search loop to test an answer. Materials: laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 (scratch.mit.edu), mini whiteboard and marker, workbook, pencil. Tutor: this deck, Scratch open for screen share. Online set-up: for the explore, children work in pairs in breakout rooms; one partner shares their screen with the machine running and types in the numbers the other partner calls out. Page 1 of the worksheet is paper only. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6, warm-up 6 to 12.5, explore at the computer 12.5 to 26.5, mini-lesson 26.5 to 34.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 34.5 to 40, worksheet 40 to 74.5 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 74.5 to 78 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 78 to 83, exit slip 83 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. SPINE: Today's tool is Work backwards. Reverse the operations from the result, then confirm by running forwards. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p6l4-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 7, 10 and 13. Every OUT is 3 more than IN. Puzzle 2: 14. Undo the + 10 first: 52 − 10 = 42. Then undo the × 3: 42 ÷ 3 = 14. Check: 3 × 14 + 10 = 52. Guessing and checking is fine. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l4-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 10. Guess my rule. Play each round live first: children call out an IN number, you say the OUT (use the rule on the card), and they guess. Then click to show the rule. Ask: "Which IN numbers helped most?" Three rounds only (the one-step n + 5 round was cut to fit the warm-up). Rounds B and C need two steps. Check the rule on EVERY pair: Round C, 1 × 3 + 2 = 5, 4 × 3 + 2 = 14, 10 × 3 + 2 = 32. Some children say "add 4" for 1 → 5: it fails at 4 → 14. Write each rule with the letter n: 5n (5 × n, we leave out the × sign), 2n − 1, 3n + 2. Round C is the machine they will build in the explore.

p6l4-warm2.note: Minutes 10 to 12.5. Whiteboards, then click. Three questions only. Answers: 1) 24 (4n means 4 × n). 2) 13 (multiply first: 18 − 5). 3) 9. Watch for 4n read as "46" in question 1, and 3n − 5 worked as 3 × 1 = 3 or as 3 × (6 − 5) = 3 in question 2.

p6l4-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 26.5 (this slide 12.5 to 18). Screen-share Scratch for 2 minutes and build the machine together: "ask" is in Sensing (light blue), "answer" is the round block under it, the * and + blocks are in Operators (green); put the * block INSIDE the + block. Make a variable called out. Type 4: it says 14. Then pairs go to breakout rooms. Each pair does ONE direction: one child changes the rule to a secret two-step rule (one × and one + or −), shares their screen and types in the IN numbers the partner calls out; the partner tries to write the rule with n using as few IN numbers as possible. The swap is the Go further what-if (below), so nobody waits. If a pair wants more: put the ask and say inside a "forever" loop so the machine keeps going; or make a three-step machine. Tutor: the Machine starter is the file L4_Function_Machine.sb3 (sent to families with the workbook; share it through the approved channel only). The child only has to change the 3 and the 2 to numbers of their own. Optional Python version (same machine, for children who know Python): n = int(input("IN? ")) | out = n * 3 + 2 | print("OUT:", out) Typing 4 prints OUT: 14; typing 10 prints OUT: 32. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): Swap jobs: now the other partner makes a secret two-step machine and you call the IN numbers. Predict which IN numbers will crack the rule fastest, then write its rule with n and check it on a pair you did not use. Answer: Numbers in a row (1, 2, 3) show the × part: OUT goes up by the × number each time. IN 0 shows the + part straight away. Rule = (× part) n + (add part), checked on a spare pair.

p6l4-explore2.note: Minutes 18 to 26.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather them. Two questions only (which IN numbers were most useful: numbers in a row, 1, 2, 3, show the × part, and IN 0 shows the + part straight away, 0 × 3 + 2 = 2, can be said in passing). Answers: 1) Times part first, then the add part: 3n + 2 means n × 3, then + 2. 2) Run it backwards: undo + 2 first (20 − 2 = 18), then undo × 3 (18 ÷ 3 = 6). Check: 6 × 3 + 2 = 20.

p6l4-teach1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 28. Teach. Click: the "+4 each time" note, then the steps. Think-aloud: "Every time n goes up by 1, OUT goes up by 4. That is what times 4 does: 4, 8, 12, 16. The 4-times table is 3 less than my OUT every time, so I add 3." Link to Lesson 1: this is the nth term idea. Always check the rule on a pair you did not use.

p6l4-we1.note: Minutes 28 to 29.5. Click through the steps. Ask before step 1: "The IN numbers jump. How can we still find the times part?" (share the OUT jump by the IN jump). Think-aloud: "IN went up 3, OUT went up 9, so each 1 in IN is worth 3 in OUT: times 3. 2 times 3 is 6, but OUT is 3, so take away 3." Check on the pair we did not use (10 → 27).

p6l4-teach2.note: Minutes 29.5 to 30.5. Teach. Ask first: "Will both machines give the same OUT for IN 4?" Thumbs up or down, then click. Remind them of the order rule from primary school: brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −. (n + 2) × 5 can also be written 5(n + 2). Do NOT say whether A and B can ever match: that is worksheet Q2(c).

p6l4-we2.note: Minutes 30.5 to 32. Click through. Analogy: "You put on socks, then shoes. To undo, shoes come off first." Think-aloud: "The machine did times 5 and then took away 4. The last thing it did was take away 4, so I undo that first: 31 + 4 = 35. Then undo times 5: 35 ÷ 5 = 7. Check forwards: 7 × 5 = 35, 35 − 4 = 31." A second one if time: (n + 2) × 5 = 45: undo × 5 first (9), then − 2: n = 7.

p6l4-try2.note: Minutes 32 to 33.5. Whiteboards. a) 43 − 7 = 36, 36 ÷ 4 = 9; check 4 × 9 + 7 = 43. b) The brackets happen first, so × 6 is the LAST step: 54 ÷ 6 = 9, 9 + 2 = 11; check (11 − 2) × 6 = 54. c) 12 − 5 = 7, 7 × 3 = 21; check 21 ÷ 3 + 5 = 12.

p6l4-key.note: Minutes 33.5 to 34.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Finding a rule from the first pair only (1 → 6 "add 5") without checking the others. (2) Undoing the steps in the wrong order, or doing the same step again instead of the opposite. (3) Reading 4n + 1 as "add 1 then times 4", or forgetting that brackets are done first.

p6l4-break.note: Minutes 34.5 to 40. 5.5 minutes. OUT jumps: 3, 5, 7, 9. Last round: "I did 11 jumps. What was my IN?" (6). Online: children stay in view of the camera and jump in place.

p6l4-ws1.note: Minutes 40 to 54. Paper only (laptops turned away). Walk around (online: visit breakout rooms). Ask "Did you check your rule on every pair?" and "Which step did you undo first?" before giving help. Show this preview, do not read it aloud.

p6l4-ws1ans.note: Minutes 54 to 57. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q3 (run the machine backwards: undo the last step first), about 35 seconds a question. Q1a: OUT is always 3 more, so n + 3 (a one-step rule). Q1d: IN goes up 1, OUT goes up 4, so × 4; 4 × 1 = 4, OUT 1, so − 3; IN 20: 80 − 3 = 77. Q2c: (n + 3) × 4 is 4n + 12, so P is always 9 more than Q (32 − 23 = 9 for IN 5): they can never match. Q3: a) 43 + 5 = 48, ÷ 6 = 8; b) 74 − 4 = 70, ÷ 7 = 10; c) 45 ÷ 5 = 9, + 3 = 12; d) 15 − 9 = 6, × 4 = 24.

p6l4-teachcode.note: Minutes 57 to 60.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4, and the second panel is the Q6 search; Q7 is the take-home question, so there is no live teaching for it). "answer" holds whatever was typed in. * means ×. The rule is OUT = 4n − 1. Ask: "Typing 0 gives a negative number. Where have we seen that before?" (Lesson 3). The last one is the machine run backwards. Python version: n = int(input("IN? ")) | out = n * 4 - 1 | print(out) (typing 5 prints 19). Second panel, Q6 plans a search: "repeat until" is in Control; the = block is in Operators. Solve 6n + 5 = 71 by trying n = 0, 1, 2, 3 … until it works: the computer is not clever, it is fast, and it stops at n = 11. Our backwards method goes straight there (71 − 5 = 66, 66 ÷ 6 = 11). If the equation has no whole-number answer, like 6n + 5 = 70, it never stops: press the red stop sign. Python: n = 0 | while n * 6 + 5 != 71: n = n + 1 | print(n) (prints 11).

p6l4-ws2.note: Minutes 60.5 to 70.5. Children work alone on Q4 to Q6; Q7 (the number trick) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Paper first, then they may build Q4 to Q6 in Scratch to test. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p6l4-ws2ans.note: Minutes 70.5 to 74.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q4 (the code and its rule). Q7 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson. Q4: OUT = 2n − 7; 2 × 3 − 7 = −1; backwards: 25 + 7 = 32, ÷ 2 = 16. Q5: n goes 1, 2, 3, 4 and then becomes 5 after the last repeat; with repeat 10 the last n is 10: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41. Q6: backwards 91 + 5 = 96, 96 ÷ 8 = 12. Q7: with 7: 12, 24, 20, 10, 3; with 10: 15, 30, 26, 13, 3. Halving 2n + 6 gives n + 3; taking away n leaves 3.

p6l4-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Answers: 1) OUT = 3n + 2 (IN up 4, OUT up 12, so × 3; 3 × 3 = 9, + 2 = 11; check 3 × 7 + 2 = 23). 2) 23 (2 → 5 → 11 → 23). 3) n = 9 (60 ÷ 4 = 15, 15 − 6 = 9; check 15 × 4 = 60).

p6l4-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 2 (2 × 3 − 4 = 2; the equation is 3n − 4 = n). 2) 15 (backwards through the second machine: 63 − 1 = 62, ÷ 2 = 31; then through the first: 31 − 1 = 30, ÷ 2 = 15. Check: 15 → 31 → 63).

p6l4-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: For Q1, fill in the table: is OUT catching up with IN? For Q2, what is in the middle box when OUT is 63?

p6l4-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the table is the computer-style search done by hand; the algebra line is optional for any pair that wants it. Q2: the middle box is 31. Extra for any pair that wants more: the two joined machines are the same as one machine "× 4, then + 3" (5 → 23: 4 × 5 + 3 = 23; 15 → 63: 4 × 15 + 3 = 63). Why? (2n + 1) × 2 + 1 = 4n + 3.

p6l4-talk.note: Minutes 78 to 83. One question only. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then volunteers share. Both get n = 9. Backwards is quicker by hand and works for big numbers (4n + 7 = 4007 would take Ravi 1000 tries). Trying every n is easy to code and also works when there is no easy backwards step, like n × n + n = 90 (n = 9). But a search must stop: if there is no whole-number answer, it would run forever. Praise answers that say WHEN each is better.

p6l4-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86. Answers: (a) 29 (6 × 4 + 5). (b) 10 (45 − 5 = 40, 40 ÷ 4 = 10; check 10 × 4 + 5 = 45). Extension: write the rule with n (4n + 5) and build it in Scratch.

p6l4-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
